## 1. Introduction

The `ODRCC` package implements estimators for a regression model in which a
covariate is **right-censored**, and the censoring depends on the outcome.

We observe

- a continuous outcome $Y$,
- fully observed covariates $Z$,
- the age at baseline $A$,
- a covariate of interest $X$ (the age at an event) that is right-censored by
  $C$, so we only observe
  $$
  W = \min(X, C), \quad \Delta = I(X \le C),
  $$
  stored in the columns `W` and `D`.

The model of interest is
$$
Y = \beta_0 + \beta_{A-X} (A - X) + \beta_Z Z + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2),
$$
where $A - X$ is the time to the event. The censoring is outcome-dependent: $C$
depends on $Y$ even once $(X, Z)$ is accounted for, and $C$ is independent of
$X$ given $(Y, Z)$.

Under outcome-dependent censoring, the complete case (CC) estimator, which
discards the rows with $\Delta = 0$, is not generally consistent. `ODRCC`
provides estimators that are consistent under outcome-dependent censoring when
the distributions they require are correctly specified:

| Function | Estimator | Consistent when correctly specified | Also uses, for efficiency only |
|---|---|---|---|
| `estimate_beta_ipw()` | IPW | $f_{C \mid Y, Z}$ | |
| `estimate_beta_mle()` | MLE | $f_{Y \mid X, Z}$ and $f_{X \mid Z}$ | |
| `estimate_beta_aipw()` | unguarded AIPW | $f_{C \mid Y, Z}$ | $f_{X \mid Y, Z}$; by default from $f_{Y \mid X, Z}$ and the $f_{X \mid Z}$ estimated by the MLE |
| `estimate_beta_aipw_lambda()` | guarded AIPW | $f_{C \mid Y, Z}$ | a working normal model for $X \mid Z$, with moments from the $f_{X \mid Z}$ estimated by the MLE |

The IPW and AIPW estimators also require a correctly specified mean model for
$Y$; the IPW and AIPW estimates of $\beta$ do not require normal errors. The MLE
requires $f_{Y \mid X, Z}$ to be correctly specified, including its normal
errors, and estimates $f_{X \mid Z}$ jointly with $\theta$. The distributions in
the last column affect only the efficiency of the AIPW estimators. The unguarded
AIPW estimator has a smaller asymptotic variance than the IPW estimator when
$f_{X \mid Y, Z}$ is correctly specified; by default, that means
$f_{Y \mid X, Z}$ and $f_{X \mid Z}$, the same distributions the MLE requires
(Section 7). The asymptotic variance of the guarded AIPW estimator never exceeds
that of the IPW estimator, whether or not its working model is correct
(Section 8). Every estimator returns estimates of $\theta = (\beta, \sigma)$ and
sandwich standard errors; the standard errors of the IPW and AIPW estimators
account for estimating $f_{C \mid Y, Z}$, and those of the MLE account for
estimating $f_{X \mid Z}$ jointly with $\theta$.

This vignette walks through an analysis with **simulated data**. The estimators
and the guidance below follow the manuscript "Matching Estimators to Effective
Sample Size Improves Inference with Outcome-Dependent Right-Censored Covariates"
by Vazquez, Ma, Marder, and Garcia.

---

## 2. Load the package and simulate data

```{r load-package}
library(ODRCC)
```

`data_aft()` simulates one dataset from the simulation design of the manuscript:
Weibull AFT models for $X \mid Z$ and $C \mid (Y, Z)$, and a normal outcome model
with $(\beta_0, \beta_{A-X}, \beta_Z) = (1, 1, 1)$ and $\sigma = 1$. The argument
`c_int` is the intercept $\tilde\eta_0$ of the model for $\log C$ and sets the
right-censoring rate; the default gives about 66%. The argument `p.c` is
$\tilde\sigma_\eta$, the scale of $\log C$. The scale of $\log X$ is
$\tilde\sigma_\gamma = 0.5$, so the default `p.c = 1.5` gives a scale ratio
$\tilde\sigma_\eta / \tilde\sigma_\gamma$ of 3.

```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(2025)
dat <- data_aft(nSubjects = 1000)

str(dat)
mean(1 - dat$D)   # right-censoring rate
```

In the simulated data,

- `y` is the outcome,
- `Z` is the covariate,
- `A` is the age at baseline,
- `X` is the age at the event (not observed when `D = 0`),
- `C` is the censoring time,
- `W` = min(X, C) and `D` = $\Delta$ = I(X ≤ C),
- `AX` = A − X is the time to the event, and `AW` = A − W,
- `b` is the subject ID.

Every estimator takes the outcome model as a formula in the column `AW`. `AW`
equals $A - X$ when $\Delta = 1$; for the censored rows, the estimators do not
use `AW` as the value of $A - X$:

```{r model-formula}
model <- y ~ AW + Z
```

The IPW and AIPW estimators also need the model for $C \mid (Y, Z)$
(`model_weights`), and the MLE and the AIPW estimators need the model for
$X \mid Z$ (`model_xz`); the MLE uses `model_weights` only for its starting
values. Both are Weibull accelerated failure time (AFT) models given as
one-sided formulas:

```{r nuisance-formulas}
model_weights <- ~ y + Z
model_xz      <- ~ Z
```

The model for $C \mid (Y, Z)$ gives $\hat\pi(t, Y, Z) = \hat P(C > t \mid Y, Z)$.
Each uncensored row $i$ receives the weight $1/\hat\pi_i$, where
$\hat\pi_i = \hat\pi(W_i, Y_i, Z_i)$ is the estimated probability that $X_i$ is
observed. The IPW and AIPW estimators use these weights; the MLE does not.

---

## 3. Effective sample size of the weights

Before choosing an estimator, compute the effective sample size (ESS) of the
weights $1/\hat\pi_i$ among the uncensored rows,
$$
\text{ESS} = \frac{\left(\sum_i \Delta_i/\hat\pi_i\right)^2}{\sum_i \Delta_i/\hat\pi_i^2},
$$
as a fraction of the number of uncensored rows (`ess_frac`). The ESS is 100%
when all weights are equal and falls as the weights become more unequal. The ESS
requires only the model for $C \mid (Y, Z)$, so the ESS can be computed before
any estimator is fit.

```{r ess}
ess <- ess_weights(dat, model_weights)
ess
```

In the manuscript's simulations, the IPW and unguarded AIPW estimators had bias
below 1% and coverage of about 92% or higher once the median ESS reached about
65%. The guarded AIPW estimator had bias below 1% once the median ESS reached
about 70%, but needed about 80% for the same coverage. The MLE uses no weights,
so its bias and coverage did not change with the ESS; the MLE depends instead on
the model for $X \mid Z$. The manuscript therefore recommends:

- ESS of at least about 65%: the IPW and unguarded AIPW estimators can be used;
- ESS of at least about 80%: the guarded AIPW estimator can be used as well;
- ESS below about 65%: the MLE is the better choice, provided the model for
  $X \mid Z$ can be specified with confidence;
- ESS below about 65% and the model for $X \mid Z$ in doubt: neither the IPW and
  AIPW estimators nor the MLE is assured to perform well.

These levels are medians across datasets from one design, with $n = 1{,}000$ and
Weibull distributions for $X$ and $C$. They are guides rather than cutoffs; the
ESS needed may differ with the sample size, the number of covariates, and these
distributions. In this dataset, the ESS is `r round(100 * ess$ess_frac)`% of the
`r ess$n_uncensored` uncensored rows: above 65% but below 80%. The guide
therefore supports the IPW and unguarded AIPW estimators here, but not yet the
guarded AIPW estimator.

---

## 4. Complete-case (CC) estimator

The **CC** estimator fits least squares to the rows with $\Delta = 1$. The CC
estimator is included for comparison.

```{r cc-estimator}
est_cc <- estimate_beta_cc(dat, model)
est_cc
```

Each estimator returns a list with

- `beta_est`: the estimates of $(\beta_0, \beta_{A-X}, \beta_Z, \sigma)$, with
  $\beta_{A-X}$ labeled `AW`, and
- `se_est`: the corresponding sandwich standard errors (`NA` for $\sigma$ from
  the CC estimator).

---

## 5. IPW estimator

The **IPW** estimator weights each uncensored row by $1/\hat\pi_i$ (Section 2).

```{r ipw-estimator}
est_ipw <- estimate_beta_ipw(dat, model, model_weights = model_weights)
est_ipw
```

`alpha_est` holds $\hat\eta$, the coefficients and scale ($\tilde\sigma_\eta$)
of the Weibull AFT model for $C \mid (Y, Z)$.

---

## 6. Maximum likelihood estimator (MLE)

The **MLE** maximizes the observed-data likelihood, integrating
$f_{Y \mid X, Z} f_{X \mid Z}$ over $x > W$ for the censored rows. The MLE
estimates the parameters $\gamma$ of the Weibull model for $X \mid Z$ together
with $\theta$, because the estimating equations for $\gamma$ involve $\theta$
through $f_{Y \mid X, Z}$. Fitting the model for $X \mid Z$ to $(W, \Delta, Z)$
alone first, as the two-step MLE does, gives a biased estimator under
outcome-dependent censoring. The MLE is consistent when $f_{Y \mid X, Z}$,
including its normal errors, and $f_{X \mid Z}$ are correctly specified. The MLE
does not use the weights; `model_weights` only sets its starting values.

```{r mle-estimator}
t_mle <- system.time(
  est_mle <- estimate_beta_mle(dat, model, model_xz = model_xz)
)
est_mle
t_mle["elapsed"]
```

`gamma_est` holds $\hat\gamma$, the coefficients and scale
($\tilde\sigma_\gamma$) of the Weibull model for $X \mid Z$; the AIPW estimators
below can reuse `gamma_est` through their `gamma` argument.

---

## 7. Unguarded AIPW estimator

The **unguarded AIPW** estimator adds to the IPW estimating equation an
augmentation term computed by numerical integration over a working model for
$f_{X \mid Y, Z}$. There are two choices for that working model:

- `fx_method = "joint"` (the default, and the choice used in the manuscript's
  simulations and application): Bayes' theorem,
  $f_{X \mid Y, Z} \propto f_{Y \mid X, Z}\, f_{X \mid Z}$, with $f_{X \mid Z}$
  estimated by the MLE;
- `fx_method = "direct"`: a Weibull AFT model for $X \mid (Y, Z)$,
  `survreg(Surv(W, D) ~ y + Z)`, fitted to all rows. Standard survival software
  can fit this model because $C$ is independent of $X$ given $(Y, Z)$. In data
  from `data_aft()`, however, $X$ given $(Y, Z)$ is not Weibull, so this model is
  misspecified here; the manuscript does not use the direct fit for that reason.

Either way, the unguarded AIPW estimator stays consistent when the model for
$C \mid (Y, Z)$ is correct; the working model affects only its efficiency. The
unguarded AIPW estimator has a smaller asymptotic variance than the IPW estimator
when two requirements hold: $f_{X \mid Y, Z}$ is correctly specified, and the
parameters $\eta$ of $f_{C \mid Y, Z}$ are independent of $\theta$. With
`fx_method = "joint"`, $f_{X \mid Y, Z}$ is correctly specified when
$f_{Y \mid X, Z}$ and $f_{X \mid Z}$ are. When either requirement does not hold,
nothing prevents the asymptotic variance of the unguarded AIPW estimator from
exceeding that of the IPW estimator.

```{r aipw-estimator}
t_aipw <- system.time(
  est_aipw <- estimate_beta_aipw(dat, model, model_xz = model_xz,
                                 model_weights = model_weights,
                                 gamma = est_mle$gamma_est)
)
est_aipw[c("beta_est", "se_est")]
t_aipw["elapsed"]

est_aipw_direct <- estimate_beta_aipw(dat, model, model_weights = model_weights,
                                      fx_method = "direct")
est_aipw_direct[c("beta_est", "se_est")]
```

When `gamma` is not supplied and `fx_method = "joint"`, `estimate_beta_aipw()`
fits the MLE first. The unguarded AIPW estimator takes longer than the MLE
(compare `t_aipw` with `t_mle`) because the unguarded AIPW estimator integrates
over $x$ for every row at each step of its solver.

---

## 8. Guarded AIPW estimator

The **guarded AIPW** estimator uses a closed-form augmentation, based on a
working normal model for $X \mid Z$ with the mean and standard deviation of the
Weibull model for $X \mid Z$ estimated by the MLE (`gamma`), and a matrix
$\Lambda$ chosen to minimize the asymptotic variance. Because of $\Lambda$, the
asymptotic variance of the guarded AIPW estimator never exceeds that of the IPW
estimator, whether or not the working model is correct. That guarantee describes
the guarded AIPW estimator as the sample size grows, not at a given ESS
(Section 3). The augmentation and the weights have closed forms, so the guarded
AIPW estimator needs no numerical integration beyond the MLE that supplies
`gamma`; when `gamma` is not supplied, `estimate_beta_aipw_lambda()` fits the
MLE first.

```{r lambda-estimator}
est_aipw_lambda <- estimate_beta_aipw_lambda(dat, model, model_xz = model_xz,
                                             model_weights = model_weights,
                                             gamma = est_mle$gamma_est)
est_aipw_lambda[c("beta_est", "se_est")]
```

---

## 9. Comparing estimators

The true values are $(\beta_0, \beta_{A-X}, \beta_Z) = (1, 1, 1)$ and
$\sigma = 1$.

```{r compare-estimators}
fits <- list(
  "CC"                     = est_cc,
  "IPW"                    = est_ipw,
  "MLE"                    = est_mle,
  "Unguarded AIPW"         = est_aipw,
  "Unguarded AIPW, direct" = est_aipw_direct,
  "Guarded AIPW"           = est_aipw_lambda
)
round(t(sapply(fits, `[[`, "beta_est")), 3)
round(t(sapply(fits, function(f) f$se_est[1:3])), 3)
```

One dataset cannot show bias. Here, each coefficient estimated by the CC
estimator is within one standard error of its true value; across 3,000 datasets
at 66% right-censoring, the CC estimator had 8.4% bias on $\beta_0$ and 82.8%
coverage (manuscript, section "Correctly specified and misspecified
distributions"). The MLE and both AIPW estimators have standard errors well below
those of the IPW estimator, and the standard errors of the MLE and the guarded
AIPW estimator are close. A small standard error alone does not make an
estimator the right choice. At the ESS of this dataset, the guide in Section 3
supports the IPW and unguarded AIPW estimators but not yet the guarded AIPW
estimator. The MLE relies instead on the model for $X \mid Z$, which is correct
here because `data_aft()` generates $X$ from a Weibull model for $X \mid Z$.

---

## 10. Reproducing the manuscript's simulations

The code that produced the simulation results in the manuscript is in the
[`simulations/`](https://github.com/jesusepfvazquez/dep-right-censored-covariate/tree/main/simulations)
folder of the repository; that code implements the estimators itself rather
than calling `ODRCC`. `data_aft()` draws the same random numbers in the same
order, so `set.seed(s); data_aft(1000, c_int)` regenerates dataset `s` (seeds 0
to 2,999) of the simulations that vary the right-censoring rate, with the
`c_int` values listed in `?data_aft`. The default `c_int = -0.5` gives the 66%
datasets of the manuscript's section "Correctly specified and misspecified
distributions". The simulations that vary the scale ratio at fixed
right-censoring rates also set `p.c`; their `c_int` values are in
`simulations/1000-CensSpread/main.R`.
